first_impression.reaction: Googled 'wedding without seating chart' on the train because I honestly don't want to do one. The intro is short and the elderly aunt line made me laugh, because that is exactly my family. Key Takeaways answered me straight away: you don't need one, it depends on the food, the room and who's coming. Then the next heading is literally my question and the answer is 'No.' Love that. I skimmed the 'instead' ideas and the FAQ, skipped the Australian allergen and Queensland bits, and I'm bookmarking it. I'm not enquiring about a planner from a seating article though.

journey.quote: Wedding Without a Seating Chart and How to Make It Work
journey.reaction: Matches what I typed. Good sign.

journey.quote: It can also leave an elderly aunt hovering with a plate while younger guests claim the good tables.
journey.reaction: Ha. Yes, this is my actual worry. Two short paragraphs and I'm at the takeaways, so no fluff problem.

journey.quote: No rule says a wedding needs a seating chart, so the decision rests on the meal service, the room and how well your guests know each other.
journey.reaction: That's the answer, first bullet. Exactly what I wanted.

journey.quote: Reserving tables for family and elders, or assigning tables rather than seats, keeps the relaxed feel while looking after the people who matter.
journey.reaction: OK this is the useful middle ground. I didn't know 'assign tables, not seats' was a thing. I could get my mum to agree to that.

journey.section: Do you need a seating chart for a wedding?
journey.quote: No. Nothing in wedding etiquette says you must have one.
journey.reaction: Heading is my question, first word is the answer. This is how every page should work.

journey.section: Do you need a seating chart for a wedding?
journey.reaction: Quick test I can actually run in my head on the train. Plated meal, yes, so maybe I need a light plan. Useful.

journey.section: Guests with allergies and dietary needs
journey.quote: In Australia, food businesses must be able to tell you about allergens
journey.reaction: And now a long list of Australian allergen rules. I'm in Singapore and I just wanted to know about chairs. Scrolling past this on my phone.

journey.quote: The same guidance advises against seating everyone who uses a wheelchair together.
journey.reaction: Fair point, but a Queensland government PDF isn't something I'd ever look at. Didn't read closely.

journey.section: What to do instead of a seating chart
journey.quote: Give each guest a table, then let them choose their chair.
journey.reaction: Short headings, one idea each. Easy to skim. This is the section I'd screenshot.

journey.quote: Ask your venue how many extra seats to set for the room and the table layout you have chosen.
journey.reaction: I was hoping for a rough rule, like 10 percent extra or something. 'Ask your venue' is fine but I wanted a number to start with.

journey.quote: Say it on your wedding website and on a welcome sign at the reception: please sit wherever you like, with family tables marked as reserved.
journey.reaction: Practical. I can basically copy that wording for our sign.

journey.section: Is it rude to have no seating chart at a wedding?
journey.quote: Not if your guests are looked after. Etiquette is about care, not paperwork.
journey.reaction: This is the line I'll send my mum.

journey.section: Is it rude to have no seating chart at a wedding?
journey.quote: In some families and cultures, where you place a parent, grandparent or elder is a sign of respect, and leaving it to chance can cause offence that lasts longer than the wedding.
journey.reaction: Very true for a lot of families I know. Nice that it's not written only for one kind of wedding.

journey.quote: It depends on the room, the table shapes and how your guests group together.
journey.reaction: Same non-answer on extra seats, now in the FAQ. The other FAQs are short and direct, this one is the weak spot.

journey.quote: Yes. Keep your own seats reserved, whether a sweetheart table, a head table with the wedding party or two places at a long table, so you never hunt for a chair.
journey.reaction: Hadn't even thought about where we'd sit. Good catch.

unanswered_questions: Roughly how many extra seats should I set with open seating? Even a rule of thumb to start with before I ask the venue.
Is any of the allergen or accessibility guidance relevant outside Australia, for example in Singapore?
When was this written or last checked? I couldn't see a date.
Does Wedded Concierge work with couples who aren't in Australia, and what does it cost? (deferred business detail)

turn_offs_found.quote: In Australia, food businesses must be able to tell you about allergens
turn_offs_found.why: A long paragraph of Australian food rules and an allergen list sits in the middle of a page about seating. On a phone it's a lot of scrolling for something that isn't my question and may not apply where I live.

turn_offs_found.quote: Ask your venue how many extra seats to set for the room and the table layout you have chosen.
turn_offs_found.why: Said twice (here and in the FAQ) with no starting figure. It's the one place the page feels like it's dodging.

would_share_with: My fiancé: the Key Takeaways and the 'What to do instead of a seating chart' list
My mum: the 'Is it rude' answer, to stop the argument

cta_reaction.quote: Your Wedded Advisor quotes in AUD for Australian couples and agrees the fee with you in writing before any work begins.
cta_reaction.why: I came for a seating question and got a great answer, so I'll bookmark the site. But I don't know this brand, I'm not planning a wedding abroad, and 'quotes in AUD for Australian couples' tells me it's probably not for me. Not handing over details from a seating article.

top_3_changes: Give a rough starting figure for extra seats (or say plainly why there isn't one) in 'Set more seats than guests' and the FAQ, so the only practical number question on the page isn't just 'ask your venue'.

Cut the allergen section down to the practical bit (give your caterer the list early, agree how special meals reach the right guest) and link out for the Australian rules, so phone readers aren't scrolling through an allergen list to get to the seating ideas.
Show a published or last-updated date near the top so I know it's current.

checks.check: Every journey point and turn-off has an exact quote from the draft
